This is the story of Group B rallying, and how it ended. Group B was introduced in 1982 as a loosely regulated class for rally manufacturers. The rules required only a small number of road-going cars be built for homologation, which let engineers chase horsepower with very few limits. Within a few seasons, manufacturers including Audi, Lancia, Peugeot, and Ford were locked in an escalating arms race, each new evolution model pushing further past what the previous generation of rally cars had ever produced. By the mid-1980s, factory Group B cars were putting out anywhere from roughly three hundred thirty to over six hundred horsepower, depending on the car and its final evolution, packed into bodies that weighed close to a thousand kilograms.
